<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Christos Kozyrakis
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>NVIDIA Research
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have recently demonstrated impressive capabilities across various embodied AI tasks.
While deploying VLA models on real-world robots imposes strict real-time inference constraints, the inference performance landscape of VLA remains poorly understood due to the large combinatorial space of model architectures and inference systems.
In this paper, we ask a fundamental research question: <span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">How should we design future VLA models and systems to support real-time inference?</span>
To address this question, we first introduce <span id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">VLA-Perf</span>, an analytical performance model that can analyze inference performance for arbitrary combinations of VLA models and inference systems.
Using <span id="abstract1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">VLA-Perf</span>, we conduct the first systematic study of the VLA inference performance landscape.
From a model-design perspective, we examine how inference performance is affected by model scaling, model architectural choices, long-context video inputs, asynchronous inference, and dual-system model pipelines.
From the deployment perspective, we analyze where VLA inference should be executed — on-device, on edge servers, or in the cloud — and how hardware capability and network performance jointly determine end-to-end latency.
By distilling 15 key takeaways from our comprehensive evaluation, we hope this work can provide practical guidance for the design of future VLA models and inference systems.</p>
  
</div><span id="footnotex1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnotetext"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">footnotetext: </span>Code available at: <a href="https://github.com/NVlabs/vla-perf" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/NVlabs/vla-perf</a>.</span></span></span>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Embodied AI is widely regarded as a promising next phase of AI, with the potential to enable physical agents that can perceive, reason, and act in the real world.
Notably, Vision–Language–Action (VLA) models have recently demonstrated strong capabilities in general-purpose manipulation tasks by integrating visual perception and language understanding into the action generation process <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zitkovich et al. (2023)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Black et al. (2024)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Intelligence et al. ()</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Amin et al. (2025)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Team et al. (2025)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bjorck et al. (2025)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To react to real-time changes in the physical world, VLA inference must operate with low latency, motivating recent work to treat inference performance<span id="footnote2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">2</span>
            
            
            
            
            
            
            
          In this paper, <span id="footnote2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">performance</span> always refers to inference latency and throughput, rather than task success rate.</span></span></span> as a first-class concern in VLA model design.
Such efforts include adopting smaller models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wen et al. (2025a)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shukor et al. (2025)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al. (2025)</a></cite> and quantization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al. (2024)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. (2025a)</a></cite>, skipping selected layers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yue et al. (2024)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al. ()</a></cite>, using fewer denoising steps in diffusion-based models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bjorck et al. (2025)</a></cite>, enabling asynchrony between model inference and robot execution <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Black et al. (2025a)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Black et al. (2025b)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sendai et al. (2025)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tang et al. (2025)</a></cite>, and adopting dual-system designs comprising two models of different scales, where only the smaller model operates at high frequency <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Figure AI (2025)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al. (2024)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Song et al. (2025)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">While these efforts on efficient VLA model design are an important step forward, we still lack a comprehensive understanding of the VLA inference performance landscape, which is determined by the vast combinatorial space of possible (1) <span id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">models</span> and (2) <span id="S1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">inference systems</span>.
Here, an <span id="S1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">inference system</span> is a combination of (a) the inference accelerator, ranging from edge GPUs to datacenter-class GPUs; (b) the location where inference is executed — on device, on server, or hybrid; and (c) for server-side inference, the wired or wireless network connecting the robot and the server.
As we will show in our evaluation, executing the same VLA model across different inference systems can lead to performance differences of multiple orders of magnitude.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">In this paper, <span id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">we present the first systematic study of VLA inference performance.</span>
This study aims to answer a simple yet fundamental question: <span id="S1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">how should we design VLA models and systems to achieve real-time inference performance?</span>
Given that standard RGB camera frame rates typically range from 24 to 60 Hz, we define a 10 Hz inference frequency as <span id="S1.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">acceptable</span> (not too far from video ingestion rates) and 100 Hz as <span id="S1.p4.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">high-performance</span> (exceeding common ingestion rates).
Based on this assumption, we further break down our research question to a series of concrete questions:</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">(1) From the perspective of VLA models, we ask: <span id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">how should future VLA models be designed under real-time performance constraints?</span>
In particular, how much can we scale up model sizes while achieving real-time inference (§<a href="#S4.SS3" title="4.3 Scaling Model Sizes Under Real-Time Constraints ‣ 4 Evaluation and Takeaways ‣ How Fast Can I Run My VLA? Demystifying VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3</span></a>)?
Are long-context VLAs that possess thousands of visual frames practically feasible (§<a href="#S4.SS4" title="4.4 Long-Context VLA Inference ‣ 4 Evaluation and Takeaways ‣ How Fast Can I Run My VLA? Demystifying VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.4</span></a>)?
How does the choice between autoregressive and diffusion-based action experts affect inference performance (§<a href="#S4.SS6" title="4.6 Diffusion-Based vs. Autoregressive Action Prediction ‣ 4 Evaluation and Takeaways ‣ How Fast Can I Run My VLA? Demystifying VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.6</span></a>)?
How do denoising steps and action chunk size influence performance (§<a href="#S4.SS5" title="4.5 Impact of Denoising Steps and Action Chunk Size ‣ 4 Evaluation and Takeaways ‣ How Fast Can I Run My VLA? Demystifying VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.5</span></a>)?
How much performance gain can be achieved through asynchronous or dual-system inference (§<a href="#S4.SS9" title="4.9 Asynchronous Inference ‣ 4 Evaluation and Takeaways ‣ How Fast Can I Run My VLA? Demystifying VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.9</span></a> and §<a href="#S4.SS10" title="4.10 Dual-system VLA Pipelines ‣ 4 Evaluation and Takeaways ‣ How Fast Can I Run My VLA? Demystifying VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.10</span></a>)?</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">(2) From a systems perspective, we ask: <span id="S1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">how should we deploy efficient inference systems for various VLA workloads?</span>
Given a model with verified accuracy, we decompose the deployment problem into the following considerations:
Where should inference be executed — on device, on server, or via device–server collaboration (§<a href="#S4.SS7" title="4.7 On-Device vs. Server-Side Inference ‣ 4 Evaluation and Takeaways ‣ How Fast Can I Run My VLA? Demystifying VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.7</span></a> and §<a href="#S4.SS8" title="4.8 Device-Server Collaborative Inference ‣ 4 Evaluation and Takeaways ‣ How Fast Can I Run My VLA? Demystifying VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.8</span></a>)?
How to choose inference hardware given the various types of available GPUs (§<a href="#S4.SS7" title="4.7 On-Device vs. Server-Side Inference ‣ 4 Evaluation and Takeaways ‣ How Fast Can I Run My VLA? Demystifying VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.7</span></a>)?
How critical is network performance in server-side inference systems (§<a href="#S4.SS7" title="4.7 On-Device vs. Server-Side Inference ‣ 4 Evaluation and Takeaways ‣ How Fast Can I Run My VLA? Demystifying VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.7</span></a>)?
What combinations of models and systems are required to support VLA inference at rates from 10 Hz up to and beyond 100 Hz (§<a href="#S4.SS11" title="4.11 Supporting High-Performance VLA Inference up to 100 Hz ‣ 4 Evaluation and Takeaways ‣ How Fast Can I Run My VLA? Demystifying VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.11</span></a>)?</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p7.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">VLA-Perf<span id="S1.p7.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_upright">.</span></span>
To enable such systematic analysis across the nearly unbounded combinatorial space of VLA models and inference systems, <span id="S1.p7.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">we develop VLA-Perf, an analytical, roofline-based performance model that predicts the optimal inference latency and throughput for arbitrary model–system combinations</span> (<a href="#S1.F1" title="In 1 Introduction ‣ How Fast Can I Run My VLA? Demystifying VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>).
<span id="S1.p7.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">VLA-Perf</span> supports a wide range of VLA configurations, including varying model sizes and architectures, stateless and long-context inference, different action chunk sizes, asynchronous inference, dual-system model pipelines.
In addition, <span id="S1.p7.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">VLA-Perf</span> supports diverse deployment scenarios, spanning inference hardware, inference locations, and network configurations.
We open-source <span id="S1.p7.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">VLA-Perf</span> to enable further performance analysis beyond those presented in this paper: <span id="S1.p7.1.6" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#FF0000;"> <a href="https://github.com/NVlabs/vla-perf" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:90%;">https://github.com/NVlabs/vla-perf</a></span>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p8.1" class="ltx_p">Using <span id="S1.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">VLA-Perf</span>, we conduct an extensive evaluation of VLA inference performance across a broad space of model variants and system designs.
From the results, we summarize <span id="S1.p8.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">15 key performance takeaways that provide practical guidance for the design of future VLA models and inference systems.</span></p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18397v1/Overview-VLA-Perf.png" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/122;" width="476" height="122" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S1.F1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic" style="font-size:90%;">VLA-Perf<span id="S1.F1.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_upright"> enables a comprehensive performance analysis of the VLA inference landscape. Our systematic study explores the interplay between model architectures and deployment configurations, yielding 15 actionable insights for designing future VLA models and serving systems.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Background and Motivation</h2>

<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Vision-Language-Action Models</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">VLA models enable embodied agents to perceive the environment through vision, reason over language instructions, and generate physical actions.
Recent VLA models have demonstrated strong performance on general-purpose manipulation tasks using robotic arms <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Brohan et al. (2022)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Black et al. (2024)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al. (2024)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al. (2023)</a></cite> and humanoid robots <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bjorck et al. (2025)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Figure AI (2025)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Model architecture.</span>
Existing VLA models adopt either <span id="S2.SS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">autoregressive-based</span> or <span id="S2.SS1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">diffusion-based (including flow matching)</span> action generation.
Autoregressive models use a single transformer to integrate visual observations, interpret language instructions, and generate actions, producing one action dimension (or token) at a time in an iterative manner.
Representative examples of this paradigm include the RT series <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Brohan et al. (2022)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zitkovich et al. (2023)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gu et al. (2023)</a></cite>, OpenVLA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al. (2024)</a></cite>, and Octo <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Team et al. (2024)</a></cite>.
More recently, an alternative VLA paradigm combines a VLM backbone with a separate, typically smaller, diffusion-based action expert.
Here, the VLM backbone ingests vision and language inputs, while a diffusion-based action expert attends to the VLM’s KV cache and generates actions through an iterative refinement process, with the number of denoising steps <span id="footnote3" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">3</span>
              
              
              
              
              
              
              
            For brevity, we use the term <em id="footnote3.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">denoising steps</em> to describe the iterative refinement steps in both classic diffusion models and flow-matching–based variants.</span></span></span> as a configurable parameter.
Representative diffusion-style VLA models include the <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> series <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Amin et al. (2025)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Intelligence et al. ()</a>; <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Black et al. (2024)</a></cite>, GR00T <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bjorck et al. (2025)</a></cite>, SmolVLA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shukor et al. (2025)</a></cite>, and TinyVLA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wen et al. (2025a)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Action prediction.</span>
Each robot action typically consists of multiple dimensions, such as joint positions, velocities, or torques for robotic arms, or whole-body joint configurations for humanoid robots.
To enable smooth and stable execution, many VLA models employ <em id="S2.SS1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">action chunking</em>, where the model predicts a sequence of future actions in a single inference <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al. (2023)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al. (2025)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jing et al. (2025)</a></cite>, with the sequence length referred to as the <span id="S2.SS1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">action chunk size</span>.
Under action chunking, an <span id="S2.SS1.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">execution horizon</span> can be specified, defined as the number of actions actually executed before the next inference is performed, which is no larger than the chunk size <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Black et al. (2025a)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Black et al. (2025b)</a></cite>.
A larger execution horizon can improve action smoothness and reduce inference frequency, but it also reduces the model’s ability to react promptly to changes in the external environment.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18397v1/Timeline.png" id="S2.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:429/96;" width="429" height="96" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S2.F2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>: </span><span id="S2.F2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">An example timeline of synchronous VLA inference. An efficient inference system should aim to match camera ingest rates to provide the robot with real-time action guidance.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Efficient VLA Inference</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">An VLA system should aim to achieve real-time inference (10 to 100 ms of latency) to match the rate of visual signal ingestion, as visualized in <a href="#S2.F2" title="In 2.1 Vision-Language-Action Models ‣ 2 Background and Motivation ‣ How Fast Can I Run My VLA? Demystifying VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.
To meet this demand, a growing number of work has proposed techniques to improve VLA inference efficiency at both the model and system levels <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al. (2025)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Reduce computation.</span>
The amount of computation can be reduced by adopting smaller models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wen et al. (2025a)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shukor et al. (2025)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al. (2025)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al. (2026)</a></cite> and quantization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al. (2024)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. (2025a)</a></cite>, skipping selected VLM layers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yue et al. (2024)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al. ()</a></cite>, or reducing the number of denoising steps in diffusion-based action experts <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bjorck et al. (2025)</a></cite>.
For autoregressive VLAs, parallel decoding can further accelerate inference by reusing KV cache for multi-token predictions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al. (2025)</a></cite>.
Finally, action chunking allows the model to predict a sequence of actions to execute in a single inference call, thereby reducing inference frequency <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al. (2023)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Black et al. (2025a)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Asynchronous inference and dual-system VLAs.</span>
Inference performance can also be improved through various forms of asynchrony.
For example, we can allow inference to begin while the robot is still executing previous actions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Black et al. (2025a)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Black et al. (2025b)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sendai et al. (2025)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tang et al. (2025)</a></cite>.
This inference-execution overlap improves GPU utilization and consequently inference throughput.
Alternatively, a dual-system VLA pipeline runs a lightweight action expert at a higher frequency (System 1) while invoking a more expensive VLM backbone at a lower frequency (System 2) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Figure AI (2025)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al. (2024)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Song et al. (2025)</a></cite>, with the two systems asynchronously exchanging latent states.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Better inference systems.</span>
While higher inference frequencies can be attained through more powerful hardware, software-level optimizations are also critical for VLA inference efficiency.
Careful CUDA-level optimizations, including CUDA graph and operator fusion, can reduce inference latency by up to <math id="S2.SS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="5\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5\times</annotation></semantics></math> compared to a naive PyTorch implementation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al. (2025)</a></cite>.
For server-side inference with action chunking, network latency and robot execution latency can be overlapped to reduce end-to-end execution time <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al. (2025)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.3 </span>Research Gap: Comprehensive Analysis of the VLA Inference Performance Landscape</h3>

<div id="S2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Despite the advances in efficient VLA designs introduced above, we still lack a comprehensive understanding of the VLA inference performance landscape, largely due to <span id="S2.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(1) the wide diversity of inference system configurations across prior studies and (2) the limited exploration of model architectures driven by inference performance concerns.</span>
From a systems perspective, VLA inference can be performed on edge GPUs integrated within the robot (on-device) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Figure AI (2025)</a></cite>, on GPU servers near the robot (edge-server) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Black et al. (2024)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Amin et al. (2025)</a></cite>, or offloaded to powerful accelerators in the cloud (cloud-server) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Brohan et al. (2022)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zitkovich et al. (2023)</a></cite> — the performance across these configurations can vary significantly, as we will show in the evaluation.
From a model-design perspective, while existing VLA models are often designed with inference efficiency in mind <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shukor et al. (2025)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wen et al. (2025a)</a></cite>, they often target specific application-system pairings.
Given the rapid evolution of both workloads and inference hardware, this approach can be myopic and can limit the exploration of alternative designs involving larger models or longer context.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Analyzing VLA Inference Performance with <span id="S3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">VLA-Perf</span></h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this paper, <span id="S3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">we aim to provide a comprehensive analysis of VLA inference performance across both existing and future, potentially hypothetical, combinations of VLA models and inference systems.</span>
Our evaluation focuses exclusively on performance characteristics — including latency and throughput — under the assumption that the underlying models meet the necessary accuracy thresholds for deployment.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">However, conducting such a comprehensive analysis is much more challenging than profiling inference performance on a small set of existing models and system implementations.
This is because it requires (1) setting up systems with various accelerator capabilities, inference locations, and network configurations, as discussed in §<a href="#S2.SS3" title="2.3 Research Gap: Comprehensive Analysis of the VLA Inference Performance Landscape ‣ 2 Background and Motivation ‣ How Fast Can I Run My VLA? Demystifying VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.3</span></a>, and (2) evaluating not only existing models but also plausible future model variants — the resulting combinatorial explosion renders exhaustive empirical evaluation both cost- and time-prohibitive.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To address this challenge, <span id="S3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">we adopt a modeling-based approach to performance analysis</span>, which has shown strong effectiveness in prior work on LLM inference and training systems <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Davies et al. (2025)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bambhaniya et al. (2024)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Agrawal et al. (2024)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cho et al. (2024)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yuan et al. (2024)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jiang et al. (2025)</a></cite>.
Analytical performance models focus on capturing the dominant performance characteristics of both the model (e.g., FLOPs and memory accesses) and the hardware (e.g., peak FLOP/s, memory bandwidth, and network bandwidth), and estimate achievable performance based on these attributes.
This approach enables fast, low-cost performance analysis across arbitrary combinations of models and hardware, without requiring the deployment of real systems.
On the downside, analytical models are not perfectly accurate, as they typically assume optimistic software implementations and therefore estimate the upper bound of achievable performance.
For example, a recent study on optimizing VLA inference performance reports that 68<math id="S3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>75% of roofline-model-predicted performance can be achieved on real systems <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al. (2025)</a></cite>.
While such predictions are not exact, we are still at an early stage in understanding VLA inference performance, and thus even coarse-grained estimates can provide valuable guidance for future model and system designs.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F3" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18397v1/transformer-ops.svg" id="S3.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/163;" width="476" height="163"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 3</span>: </span><span id="S3.F3.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic" style="font-size:90%;">VLA-Perf<span id="S3.F3.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_upright"> abstracts VLA inference as model components interleaved with data transfers.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">VLA-Perf<span id="S3.p4.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_upright"> overview.</span></span>
We build <span id="S3.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">VLA-Perf</span>, a roofline-based analytical performance model for VLA inference.
Figure <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3 Analyzing VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf ‣ How Fast Can I Run My VLA? Demystifying VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> illustrates an example VLA inference workflow, which consists of a robot and multiple model components.
Depending on the placement of each model component (either on the robot or on a server), these components exchange data either locally or over a network.
Such data transfers may include raw images, vision tokens, KV caches, or action predictions.
Each model component is abstracted as a sequence of operators, such as fully connected layers, linear projections, and attention blocks.
<span id="S3.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">VLA-Perf</span> assumes that inference for each individual model component (e.g., the VLM backbone) is executed on a single accelerator, because modern GPUs, including recent edge accelerators, already provide sufficient memory capacity to host complete VLA models, for example up to 128 GB on NVIDIA Jetson Thor.
On the contrary, different model components can be executed either on the same accelerator or on different accelerators.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F4" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">

<div id="lstnumberx14" class="ltx_listingline">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F4.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 4</span>: </span><span id="S3.F4.7" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Example inputs to <span id="S3.F4.7.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">VLA-Perf</span>, including model parameters (left) and system specifications (right).</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Input parameters.</span>
<span id="S3.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">VLA-Perf</span> enables the analysis of arbitrary model-system combinations by parameterizing both model and system parameters, with an example provided in <a href="#S3.F4" title="In 3 Analyzing VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf ‣ How Fast Can I Run My VLA? Demystifying VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>.
On the model side, these parameters include the choice of vision encoder, VLM backbone, and action expert; the input and output sequence lengths of each model; the number of denoising steps for diffusion-based action experts; action chunk size; and the dimensionality of each action.
On the system side, <span id="S3.p5.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">VLA-Perf</span> supports various inference accelerators of configurable peak FLOP/s and memory bandwidth, as well as network systems characterized by upload/download bandwidth and latency.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Latency calculation.</span>
Given the inputs above, the end-to-end inference latency of a VLA system is modeled as the sum of model inference latency and data movement latency across all components:</p>
<table id="S3.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T_{\text{total}}=\sum_{m\in\mathcal{M}}T_{m}+\sum_{d\in\mathcal{D}}T_{d}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mtext>total</mtext></msub><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi></mrow></munder><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em">+</mo><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi></mrow></munder><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T_{\text{total}}=\sum_{m\in\mathcal{M}}T_{m}+\sum_{d\in\mathcal{D}}T_{d},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.p6.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the set of model inference components and <math id="S3.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the set of data movement stages.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p7.1" class="ltx_p">For a single model component <math id="S3.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math>, the inference latency <math id="S3.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T_{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T_{m}</annotation></semantics></math> is modeled as the sum of latency of each of its constituent operators:</p>
<table id="S3.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T_{m}=\sum_{o\in\mathcal{O}_{m}}T_{o}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></mrow></munder><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>o</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T_{m}=\sum_{o\in\mathcal{O}_{m}}T_{o},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.p7.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.p7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}_{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}_{m}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the sequence of operators in model <math id="S3.p7.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math>.
For each operator <math id="S3.p7.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="o" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>o</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">o</annotation></semantics></math>, <span id="S3.p7.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">VLA-Perf</span> models its execution latency using a roofline model that accounts for both compute and memory access latency:</p>
<table id="S3.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T_{o}=\max\left(\frac{\text{FLOPs}_{o}}{\text{FLOP/s}_{h}},\frac{\text{Bytes}_{o}}{\text{MemBW}_{h}}\right)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>o</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>max</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac><msub><mtext>FLOPs</mtext><mi>o</mi></msub><msub><mtext>FLOP/s</mtext><mi>h</mi></msub></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mfrac><msub><mtext>Bytes</mtext><mi>o</mi></msub><msub><mtext>MemBW</mtext><mi>h</mi></msub></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T_{o}=\max\left(\frac{\text{FLOPs}_{o}}{\text{FLOP/s}_{h}},\frac{\text{Bytes}_{o}}{\text{MemBW}_{h}}\right),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.p7.3" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.p7.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{FLOPs}_{o}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mtext>FLOPs</mtext><mi>o</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{FLOPs}_{o}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.p7.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{Bytes}_{o}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mtext>Bytes</mtext><mi>o</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{Bytes}_{o}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the total floating-point operations and memory bytes accessed by operator <math id="S3.p7.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="o" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>o</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">o</annotation></semantics></math>, while <math id="S3.p7.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{FLOP/s}_{a}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mtext>FLOP/s</mtext><mi>a</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{FLOP/s}_{a}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.p7.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{MemBW}_{a}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mtext>MemBW</mtext><mi>a</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{MemBW}_{a}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the peak compute throughput and memory bandwidth of the inference hardware <math id="S3.p7.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math>, respectively.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p8.1" class="ltx_p">We assume that local data movement on the same accelerator is sufficiently fast to be treated as negligible, while network-based data movement between devices is modeled as:</p>
<table id="S3.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T_{d}^{\text{net}}=\text{NetLat}+\frac{\text{Bytes}_{d}}{\text{NetBW}}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>T</mi><mi>d</mi><mtext>net</mtext></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mtext>NetLat</mtext><mo>+</mo><mfrac><msub><mtext>Bytes</mtext><mi>d</mi></msub><mtext>NetBW</mtext></mfrac></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T_{d}^{\text{net}}=\text{NetLat}+\frac{\text{Bytes}_{d}}{\text{NetBW}},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.p8.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.p8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{Bytes}_{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mtext>Bytes</mtext><mi>d</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{Bytes}_{d}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the amount of transferred data, and <span id="S3.p8.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_markedasmath">NetBW</span> and <span id="S3.p8.2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_markedasmath">NetLat</span> denote the single-directional network bandwidth and latency, respectively.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.T1" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption" style="font-size:80%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S3.T1.9" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:113%;">Table 1</span>: </span><span id="S3.T1.10" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:113%;">Roofline model validation against real <math id="S3.T1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> Triton inference latencies on an RTX 4090 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al. <div id="S3.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p9.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p9.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Modeling fidelity.</span>
Due to the scarcity of well-optimized frameworks for VLA inference, we mainly validate the fidelity of <span id="S3.p9.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">VLA-Perf</span> using the <math id="S3.p9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> implementation by Ma et al. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al. (2025)</a></cite>, a Triton-based implementation specifically tuned for RTX 4090.
<a href="#S3.T1" title="In 3 Analyzing VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf ‣ How Fast Can I Run My VLA? Demystifying VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> compares the performance predicted by <span id="S3.p9.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">VLA-Perf</span> to the empirical measurements conducted by Ma et al. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al. (2025)</a></cite>.
The results demonstrate that an optimized system can achieve <math id="S3.p9.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="73.3\sim 82.6\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>73.3</mn><mo>∼</mo><mrow><mn>82.6</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">73.3\sim 82.6\%</annotation></semantics></math> of the theoretical roofline reported by <span id="S3.p9.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">VLA-Perf</span>, with the gap narrowing as the workload increases (e.g., when processing three camera frames).</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p10" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p10.1" class="ltx_p">The performance differences between a real inference system and the roofline limits reported by <span id="S3.p10.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">VLA-Perf</span> are due to both hardware and software factors.
First, <span id="S3.p10.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">VLA-Perf</span> abstracts away hardware-specific details, including microarchitectural design, instruction scheduling, and memory-access behavior.
Instead, <span id="S3.p10.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">VLA-Perf</span> assumes that the maximum theoretical compute capability and memory bandwidth are attainable for every operator executed.
Second, real-world systems incur software overheads, such as kernel launch latencies, operating system interference, and runtime library overhead, which are not explicitly modeled by <span id="S3.p10.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">VLA-Perf</span>.
Nevertheless, we believe that a modeling fidelity exceeding 80% is sufficient to provide meaningful insights into the VLA performance landscape, and thus leave the tuning of <span id="S3.p10.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">VLA-Perf</span> for specific hardware and software platforms, such as in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Davies et al. (2025)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jiang et al. (2025)</a></cite>, to future work.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Evaluation and Takeaways</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we use <span id="S4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">VLA-Perf</span> to conduct a comprehensive analysis of VLA inference performance.
Our evaluation is structured to address two sets of research questions as below.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Question 1: How should we design future VLA models to meet real-time latency constraints?</span></p>
<ul id="S4.I1" class="ltx_itemize" style="--ltx-enum-leftmargin:1.2em;">
<li id="S4.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">How far can model sizes be scaled while still enabling real-time inference (§<a href="#S4.SS3" title="4.3 Scaling Model Sizes Under Real-Time Constraints ‣ 4 Evaluation and Takeaways ‣ How Fast Can I Run My VLA? Demystifying VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3</span></a>)?</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Are long-context VLAs that process thousands of visual frames practically feasible (§<a href="#S4.SS4" title="4.4 Long-Context VLA Inference ‣ 4 Evaluation and Takeaways ‣ How Fast Can I Run My VLA? Demystifying VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.4</span></a>)?</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">How do autoregressive and diffusion-based action experts compare in performance (§<a href="#S4.SS6" title="4.6 Diffusion-Based vs. Autoregressive Action Prediction ‣ 4 Evaluation and Takeaways ‣ How Fast Can I Run My VLA? Demystifying VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.6</span></a>)?</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">How do denoising steps and action chunk size influence performance (§<a href="#S4.SS5" title="4.5 Impact of Denoising Steps and Action Chunk Size ‣ 4 Evaluation and Takeaways ‣ How Fast Can I Run My VLA? Demystifying VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.5</span></a>)?</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i5" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Are asynchronous or dual-system inference much faster than synchronous inference (§<a href="#S4.SS9" title="4.9 Asynchronous Inference ‣ 4 Evaluation and Takeaways ‣ How Fast Can I Run My VLA? Demystifying VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.9</span></a> and §<a href="#S4.SS10" title="4.10 Dual-system VLA Pipelines ‣ 4 Evaluation and Takeaways ‣ How Fast Can I Run My VLA? Demystifying VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.10</span></a>)?</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Question 2: How should inference systems be deployed for different VLA workloads?</span></p>
<ul id="S4.I2" class="ltx_itemize" style="--ltx-enum-leftmargin:1.2em;">
<li id="S4.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Should inference be executed on device, on server, or via device-server collaboration (§<a href="#S4.SS7" title="4.7 On-Device vs. Server-Side Inference ‣ 4 Evaluation and Takeaways ‣ How Fast Can I Run My VLA? Demystifying VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.7</span></a> and §<a href="#S4.SS8" title="4.8 Device-Server Collaborative Inference ‣ 4 Evaluation and Takeaways ‣ How Fast Can I Run My VLA? Demystifying VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.8</span></a>)?</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">How capable must inference hardware be to meet real-time performance requirements (§<a href="#S4.SS7" title="4.7 On-Device vs. Server-Side Inference ‣ 4 Evaluation and Takeaways ‣ How Fast Can I Run My VLA? Demystifying VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.7</span></a>)?</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I2.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I2.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I2.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">How critical is network performance for server-side inference systems (§<a href="#S4.SS7" title="4.7 On-Device vs. Server-Side Inference ‣ 4 Evaluation and Takeaways ‣ How Fast Can I Run My VLA? Demystifying VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.7</span></a>)?</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I2.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span>

<p id="S4.I2.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">What model-system combinations can achieve inference rates from 10 Hz to 100 Hz (§<a href="#S4.SS11" title="4.11 Supporting High-Performance VLA Inference up to 100 Hz ‣ 4 Evaluation and Takeaways ‣ How Fast Can I Run My VLA? Demystifying VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.11</span></a>)?</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S4.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Our experiments are organized as follows.
§<a href="#S4.SS2" title="4.2 Baseline 𝜋_0 Inference Latency Across Hardware Backends ‣ 4 Evaluation and Takeaways ‣ How Fast Can I Run My VLA? Demystifying VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.2</span></a> presents a baseline analysis of the <math id="S4.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> model.
§<a href="#S4.SS3" title="4.3 Scaling Model Sizes Under Real-Time Constraints ‣ 4 Evaluation and Takeaways ‣ How Fast Can I Run My VLA? Demystifying VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3</span></a><math id="S4.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math><a href="#S4.SS6" title="4.6 Diffusion-Based vs. Autoregressive Action Prediction ‣ 4 Evaluation and Takeaways ‣ How Fast Can I Run My VLA? Demystifying VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.6</span></a> explore various model configuration to examine their impact on inference performance.
§<a href="#S4.SS7" title="4.7 On-Device vs. Server-Side Inference ‣ 4 Evaluation and Takeaways ‣ How Fast Can I Run My VLA? Demystifying VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.7</span></a><math id="S4.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math><a href="#S4.SS11" title="4.11 Supporting High-Performance VLA Inference up to 100 Hz ‣ 4 Evaluation and Takeaways ‣ How Fast Can I Run My VLA? Demystifying VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.11</span></a> additionally considers inference placement and network latency, closely reflecting real-world deployments.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Evaluation Setup</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We describe the main model and system settings here, with additional details provided in Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Detailed System and Model Parameters ‣ How Fast Can I Run My VLA? Demystifying VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Models and robot.</span>
We evaluate a set of model variants derived from the <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> architecture <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Black et al. (2024)</a></cite>, which we choose due to its strong robotic task performance and widespread adoption in recent VLA systems.
The original <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> model consists of a 400M SigLIP vision encoder, a 2B Gemma language model, and a 300M diffusion-based action expert.
Throughout the experiments, we consider a bimanual robotic manipulation setting, which is common for both stationary robots and mobile platforms such as wheeled or humanoid robots.
With the UR5e robot arm, this setup is equipped with three cameras and an action space of 14 degrees of freedom (DoF).
Each camera image has a resolution of 224<math id="S4.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>224 and is tokenized into 256 visual tokens, yielding 768 visual tokens across three cameras.
Assuming 32 language tokens per task, the total input sequence length per inference is 800 tokens.
Unless otherwise specified, we use an action chunk size of 50 and 10 denoising steps for action generation, same as the original <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> configuration.</p>
</div>

</figure>
<div id="S4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Inference systems.</span>
We evaluate a range of accelerators spanning high-end edge GPUs (e.g., NVIDIA Jetson Thor), consumer-grade GPUs commonly used in research experiments (e.g., RTX 4090), and high-end datacenter GPUs, including A100, H100, and B100.
The GPUs can be mapped to various inference location as shown in <a href="#S4.T2" title="In 4.1 Evaluation Setup ‣ 4 Evaluation and Takeaways ‣ How Fast Can I Run My VLA? Demystifying VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.
For server-side inference, we evaluate both wired and wireless network configurations, including Ethernet, WiFi, and cellular (4G/5G) networks.
All experiments assume BF16 for inference, or FP16 when BF16 is not supported by the hardware.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Performance metrics.</span>
We report VLA system latency, defined as the elapsed time from when the robot perceives visual observations to when the robot receives the corresponding action prediction.
We also report throughput in Hertz (Hz), defined as the number of inferences that can be executed per second at a batch size of one (i.e., a single robot).
For synchronous inference, throughput is the inverse of inference latency, whereas for asynchronous inference, throughput can exceed the inverse latency.
We report inference performance independent of robot execution latency, as the latter is highly robot-dependent.
Furthermore, the effective action execution frequency may exceed the inference frequency due to action chunking — with a chunk size of five, the robot can execute actions at up to five actions given a single inference.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Baseline <math id="S4.SS2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> Inference Latency Across Hardware Backends</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Before evaluating model and system variants, we first establish a baseline by measuring the inference performance of the <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> model across a range of GPUs, without considering network latency.</p>
</div>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption" style="font-size:80%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S4.T4.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:113%;">Table 4</span>: </span><span id="S4.T4.7" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:113%;">Compute- vs. memory-bound analysis of <math id="S4.T4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> across different hardware. Operator intensity (OI) denotes the ratio between compute operations and memory accesses (FLOPs/Bytes). The balance OI denotes the hardware balance point at which compute throughput and memory bandwidth are equally limiting.</span></figcaption>

<span id="S4.T4.8.1.5.4.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_middle" style="width:51.0pt;">
<span id="S4.T4.8.1.5.4.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center"><span id="S4.T4.8.1.5.4.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">Compute</span></span>
</span></td>
<td id="S4.T4.8.1.5.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_middle ltx_border_t">
<span id="S4.T4.8.1.5.5.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_middle" style="width:51.0pt;">
<span id="S4.T4.8.1.5.5.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center"><span id="S4.T4.8.1.5.5.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">Memory</span></span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S4.T4.8.1.6" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S4.T4.8.1.6.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_middle ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t">
<span id="S4.T4.8.1.6.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_middle" style="width:42.5pt;">
<span id="S4.T4.8.1.6.1.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_left"><span id="S4.T4.8.1.6.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">B100</span></span>
</span></td>

</span></td>
<td id="S4.T4.8.1.6.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_middle ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t">

</span></td>
<td id="S4.T4.8.1.6.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_middle ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t">
<span id="S4.T4.8.1.6.4.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_middle" style="width:51.0pt;">
<span id="S4.T4.8.1.6.4.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center"><span id="S4.T4.8.1.6.4.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">Compute</span></span>
</span></td>
<td id="S4.T4.8.1.6.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_middle ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t">

<span id="S4.T4.8.1.6.5.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center"><span id="S4.T4.8.1.6.5.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">Memory</span></span>
</span></td></tr>
</table>
</span></div>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_ulem_uline ltx_font_italic">Takeaway 1: Existing datacenter GPUs can already achieve inference frequencies comparable to camera frame rates for small VLA models such as <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>, while edge GPUs remain performance-limited.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#S4.T3" title="In 4.2 Baseline 𝜋_0 Inference Latency Across Hardware Backends ‣ 4 Evaluation and Takeaways ‣ How Fast Can I Run My VLA? Demystifying VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> shows that A100, H100, and B100 achieve inference frequencies ranging from 61.7 Hz to 314.4 Hz, which are at least on par with the frame rates of common RGB cameras (24<math id="S4.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>60 Hz).
In contrast, Jetson Thor achieve substantially lower inference frequency (19.0 Hz), falling below the frame rates of most cameras.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_ulem_uline ltx_font_italic">Takeaway 2: Action prediction is memory-bound across hardware, while vision and VLM inference are compute-bound on most GPUs except from Jetson Thor.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#S4.T4" title="In 4.2 Baseline 𝜋_0 Inference Latency Across Hardware Backends ‣ 4 Evaluation and Takeaways ‣ How Fast Can I Run My VLA? Demystifying VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> summarizes the workload characteristics of each VLA model component.
The vision encoder and the VLM backbone exhibit significantly higher operator intensity (321.4 and 542.8 FLOPs/Byte, respectively) compared to the action expert (54.0 FLOPs/Byte).
This is because the vision encoder and the VLM backbone process many input tokens (e.g., 768 for SigLIP and 800 for Gemma), inherently batching computation across tokens, whereas the diffusion-based action expert operates on far fewer tokens (e.g., the same as the action chunk size of 50).
This behavior closely mirrors LLM inference, where the prefill phase (prompt processing) is compute-intensive, while the decode phase (token generation) is memory-bound <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Patel et al. (2024)</a></cite>.
Jetson Thor, in contrast to the other evaluated GPUs, relies on LPDDR memory, which prioritizes low power consumption for embedded devices but provides substantially lower bandwidth (270 GB/s) than GDDR on RTX 4090 (1 TB/s) and HBM on B100 (8 TB/s).
As a result, even the vision encoder and VLM backbone become memory-bound on Jetson Thor.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Scaling Model Sizes Under Real-Time Constraints</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We next study how inference latency scales with increasing VLA model sizes, which are positively correlated with task accuracy <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Team (2025)</a></cite>.
Specifically, we scale each component of the <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> model and construct a family of larger VLA models.
For the vision encoder, we replace the original SigLIP-So400m used in <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> with the larger SigLIP-Giant model with 1.1B parameters.
For the VLM, we replace Gemma with the Llama2 family (7B, 13B, and 70B), which provides a wider range of model scales.
For the action expert, we follow the <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> design principle and instantiate it as a scaled-down version of the corresponding VLM, with approximately <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m4" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="4\sim 8\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo>∼</mo><mn>8</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4\sim 8\times</annotation></semantics></math> fewer parameters by reducing the transformer hidden dimension and intermediate dimension by <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m5" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="2\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\times</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m6" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="4\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4\times</annotation></semantics></math>, respectively.
By combining these components, we construct a set of hypothetical larger VLA models, denoted as <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>-L, <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>-XL, and <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>-XXL, whose configurations are summarized in <a href="#S4.T5" title="In 4.3 Scaling Model Sizes Under Real-Time Constraints ‣ 4 Evaluation and Takeaways ‣ How Fast Can I Run My VLA? Demystifying VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T5" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S4.T5.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 5</span>: </span><span id="S4.T5.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Inference performance of scaled-up VLA models across different hardware platforms.</span></figcaption>

</span></td>

</span></td></tr>
