</figure>
<figure id="S4.F5" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18397v1/pi0_model_scaling_components.svg" id="S4.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/139;" width="476" height="139"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F5.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 5</span>: </span><span id="S4.F5.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Increased model sizes lead to proportional inference latency increases.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_ulem_uline ltx_font_italic">Takeaway 3: Latency of each VLA component scales approximately linearly with increasing model sizes.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#S4.F5" title="In 4.3 Scaling Model Sizes Under Real-Time Constraints ‣ 4 Evaluation and Takeaways ‣ How Fast Can I Run My VLA? Demystifying VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> breaks down the inference latency of individual VLA components as model size increases, where both axes are shown on a logarithmic scale.
Across all components, larger models impose proportionally higher computational costs, and thus inference latency grows approximately linearly with model size.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS3.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_ulem_uline ltx_font_italic">Takeaway 4: While edge and consumer GPUs struggle with larger models, datacenter GPUs can still support real-time inference for VLA models that are more than one order of magnitude larger.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#S4.T5" title="In 4.3 Scaling Model Sizes Under Real-Time Constraints ‣ 4 Evaluation and Takeaways ‣ How Fast Can I Run My VLA? Demystifying VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> summarizes inference performance across different model scales.
B100 sustains 9.6 Hz inference even for the largest 81B model variant (30<math id="S4.SS3.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> larger than <math id="S4.SS3.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>), demonstrating that modern datacenter GPUs can accommodate substantially larger VLA models under real-time constraints.
In contrast, RTX 4090 runs out of memory for <math id="S4.SS3.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>-XL (16.7B), and Jetson Thor struggles to deliver real-time performance even with sufficient memory capacity, achieving only 2.1 Hz inference frequency on <math id="S4.SS3.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>-XL.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.4 </span>Long-Context VLA Inference</h3>

<div id="S4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">While <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> model ipredicts actions solely based on the current observation, this a memory-less design is insufficient for long-horizon tasks that require reasoning over temporal context <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jang et al. (2025)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shi et al. (2025)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Team et al. (2024)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. (2025b)</a></cite>.
In this section, we adapt <math id="S4.SS4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> to a stateful setting by enabling it to incorporate past visual states into the VLM KV cache.
At each new timestep, the latest visual inputs (three camera images, corresponding to 768 vision tokens) attend over the accumulated KV cache of the VLM, and the action prediction is conditioned on this long context.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_ulem_uline ltx_font_italic">Takeaway 5: Datacenter GPUs can support real-time long-context VLA inference with up to 1K past timesteps, while edge and consumer GPUs are limited to roughly 100 steps.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#S4.T6" title="In 4.4 Long-Context VLA Inference ‣ 4 Evaluation and Takeaways ‣ How Fast Can I Run My VLA? Demystifying VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> reports inference performance and memory consumption of long-context VLA with up to 10K past timesteps.
B100 sustains 11.7 Hz inference with 1K past timesteps, whereas performance drops to 1.2 Hz at 10K steps, which no longer meets real-time requirements.
For Jetson Thor and RTX 4090, real-time performance is only achievable when the context length is limited to roughly 100 timesteps (around 8 Hz).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T6" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S4.T6.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 6</span>: </span><span id="S4.T6.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Inference performance and memory consumption of long-context VLA models.</span></figcaption>

<td id="S4.T6.5.1.5.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_middle ltx_border_t">

</span></td></tr>

</table>
</span></div>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.5 </span>Impact of Denoising Steps and Action Chunk Size</h3>

<div id="S4.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Given a diffusion-based action expert model, two key parameters influence inference performance: (1) the number of denoising steps, where each step incurs a forward pass, and (2) the action chunk size, i.e., the number of predicted actions.
To this end, we vary the number of diffusion steps of <math id="S4.SS5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> from 1 to 50 (default: 10) and the action chunk size from 5 to 250 (default: 50), each spanning a <math id="S4.SS5.p1.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="50\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>50</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">50\times</annotation></semantics></math> range.
For brevity, we present results on B100, but the observed trends below are consistent across all evaluated GPUs.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_ulem_uline ltx_font_italic">Takeaway 6: Denoising steps have a significant impact on both action expert latency and end-to-end VLA latency, whereas action chunk size has a negligible effect.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS5.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#S4.F6.sf1" title="In Figure 6 ‣ 4.5 Impact of Denoising Steps and Action Chunk Size ‣ 4 Evaluation and Takeaways ‣ How Fast Can I Run My VLA? Demystifying VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6(a)</span></a> and <a href="#S4.F6.sf2" title="In Figure 6 ‣ 4.5 Impact of Denoising Steps and Action Chunk Size ‣ 4 Evaluation and Takeaways ‣ How Fast Can I Run My VLA? Demystifying VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6(b)</span></a> report the action expert latency and end-to-end VLA inference latency, respectively.
On the one hand, action prediction latency scales linearly with the number of diffusion steps and thus has a substantial impact on overall VLA latency.
For example, with the default action chunk size of 50, increasing the number of diffusion steps from 10 to 50 leads to a proportional increase in action prediction latency (<math id="S4.SS5.p3.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="5\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5\times</annotation></semantics></math>) and a <math id="S4.SS5.p3.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="2.15\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2.15</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2.15\times</annotation></semantics></math> increase in overall VLA latency.
On the other hand, action chunk size has only a marginal effect on both action-expert latency and end-to-end VLA inference latency.
With the default setting of 10 denoising steps, increasing the action chunk size from 50 to 250 (<math id="S4.SS5.p3.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="5\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5\times</annotation></semantics></math>) increases action prediction latency by only 40%, resulting in just an 11% increase in end-to-end VLA latency.
This is because action prediction is typically memory-bound (<a href="#S4.F6.sf3" title="In Figure 6 ‣ 4.5 Impact of Denoising Steps and Action Chunk Size ‣ 4 Evaluation and Takeaways ‣ How Fast Can I Run My VLA? Demystifying VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6(c)</span></a>): performance is limited by loading model parameters and KV cache from memory, and the additional computation given more action tokens has little effect on overall latency.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F6" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_3">
<figure id="S4.F6.sf1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><img src="2602.18397v1/pi0_denoise_steps_action_lengths_diffusion_relative_B100.png" id="S4.F6.sf1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/330;" width="476" height="330" alt="Refer to caption">

</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_3">
<figure id="S4.F6.sf2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><img src="2602.18397v1/pi0_denoise_steps_action_lengths_e2e_relative_B100.png" id="S4.F6.sf2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/329;" width="476" height="329" alt="Refer to caption">

</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_3">

</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F6.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 6</span>: </span><span id="S4.F6.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">The impact of denoising steps and action chunk sizes to inference performance on B100 GPU.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS6" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.6 </span>Diffusion-Based vs. Autoregressive Action Prediction</h3>

<div id="S4.SS6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Diffusion-based and autoregressive action prediction are two dominant paradigms in recent VLA models.
Autoregressive action decoder typically uses the same transformer to process vision and language inputs and to generate actions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al. (2024)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Team et al. (2024)</a></cite>.
Accordingly, we adapt <math id="S4.SS6.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> to an autoregressive variant that uses the VLM backbone directly for action prediction.
In contrast, diffusion-based VLAs usually employ a separate action expert that is significantly smaller than the VLM (e.g., <math id="S4.SS6.p1.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="6.7\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>6.7</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">6.7\times</annotation></semantics></math> smaller in <math id="S4.SS6.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Black et al. (2024)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bjorck et al. (2025)</a></cite>.
For fairness, we additionally evaluate a diffusion-based variant with an action expert that matches the VLM size, referred to as <span id="S4.SS6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Diffusion-Large</span>.
Classic autoregressive VLAs generate one action dimension at a time, which results in high inference latency as it requires many sequential prediction steps (e.g., 700 steps in our case with a 14-DoF action space and an action chunk size of 50).
Thus, we also evaluate a faster autoregressive variant with parallel decoding <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al. (2025)</a></cite>, which predicts all actions in a single inference, denoted as <span id="S4.SS6.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Autoregressive-Parallel</span>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS6.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS6.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS6.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_ulem_uline ltx_font_italic">Takeaway 7: With action chunking, diffusion-based VLA inference is one to two orders of magnitude faster than the vanilla autoregressive VLA.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS6.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS6.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#S4.F7.sf1" title="In Figure 7 ‣ 4.6 Diffusion-Based vs. Autoregressive Action Prediction ‣ 4 Evaluation and Takeaways ‣ How Fast Can I Run My VLA? Demystifying VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7(a)</span></a> compares inference latency across different architectures on the B100 GPU.
Across all action chunk sizes, diffusion-based models (both the standard and large variants) consistently outperform the vanilla autoregressive VLA.
With the default chunk size of 50, the standard diffusion model achieves an inference latency of 3.2 ms, which is <math id="S4.SS6.p3.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="102.4\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>102.4</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">102.4\times</annotation></semantics></math> faster than the classic autoregressive model (327.6 ms).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS6.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS6.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS6.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_ulem_uline ltx_font_italic">Takeaway 8: Autoregressive VLAs are competitive only when generating a small number of action tokens or when parallel decoding is enabled.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS6.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS6.p5.1" class="ltx_p">To further analyze scenarios where autoregressive VLAs can be efficient, we evaluate inference performance without action chunking across common action dimensionalities, ranging from 7 DoF for a single robot arm <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Black et al. (2024)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zitkovich et al. (2023)</a></cite> to over 40 DoF for two dexterous hands <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wen et al. (2025b)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Christoph et al. (2025)</a></cite>.
As shown in <a href="#S4.F7.sf2" title="In Figure 7 ‣ 4.6 Diffusion-Based vs. Autoregressive Action Prediction ‣ 4 Evaluation and Takeaways ‣ How Fast Can I Run My VLA? Demystifying VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7(b)</span></a>, the autoregressive model can slightly outperform the large diffusion-based model when the number of generated action tokens is small (e.g., 7), although the standard-size diffusion model remains faster.
Another scenario in which autoregressive inference becomes competitive is when parallel decoding is employed.
As shown in <a href="#S4.F7.sf1" title="In Figure 7 ‣ 4.6 Diffusion-Based vs. Autoregressive Action Prediction ‣ 4 Evaluation and Takeaways ‣ How Fast Can I Run My VLA? Demystifying VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7(a)</span></a>, parallel decoding outperforms the standard diffusion model for action chunk sizes up to 10.
However, for larger chunk sizes such as 50, the latency of parallel decoding increases substantially as the workload transitions from memory-bound to compute-bound (OI increases from 135.9 at chunk size 10 to 477.7 at chunk size 50, exceeding the B100 balance OI of 218.8).
In contrast, the diffusion-based action expert remains memory-bound (OI = 54.0 at chunk size of 50), leading to more stable inference performance across chunk sizes.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F7" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S4.F7.sf1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18397v1/pi0_autoregressive_vs_diffusion_chunk_size_B100.svg" id="S4.F7.sf1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/314;" width="476" height="314"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F7.sf1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">(a)</span> </span><span id="S4.F7.sf1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Varying action chunk sizes.</span></figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S4.F7.sf2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18397v1/pi0_autoregressive_vs_diffusion_dof_B100.svg" id="S4.F7.sf2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/315;" width="476" height="315"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F7.sf2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">(b)</span> </span><span id="S4.F7.sf2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Varying DoF (no action chunking).</span></figcaption>
</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F7.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 7</span>: </span><span id="S4.F7.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Diffusion vs autoregressive VLA inference performance on B100 GPU.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS7" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.7 </span>On-Device vs. Server-Side Inference</h3>

<div id="S4.SS7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate three classes of VLA inference systems with different GPU and network configurations.
First, <em id="S4.SS7.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">on-device inference</em>, where inference is executed directly on an edge GPU integrated into the robot (e.g., Jetson Thor), as demonstrated by systems such as Figure AI’s Helix <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Figure AI (2025)</a></cite>.
Second, <em id="S4.SS7.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">edge-server inference</em>, where inference is performed on a server located close to the robot <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Black et al. (2024)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bjorck et al. (2025)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al. (2025)</a></cite>.
In this setting, communication between the robot and the server may use wired networks (Ethernet) for fixed-base robots or wireless networks (WiFi or cellular networks) for mobile robots (e.g., wheeled or humanoid robots), while the server-side accelerator may range from consumer-grade GPUs (e.g., RTX 4090) to datacenter-class GPUs (e.g., B100).
Third, <em id="S4.SS7.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">cloud-server inference</em>, where inference runs on high-end datacenter GPUs.
In this case, the robot first communicates with a nearby gateway server via a wired or wireless connection, which then forwards inference requests to the cloud, incurring two stages of communication latency.
Note that network latency to cloud servers can vary substantially, depending on factors such as physical distance and routing topology <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mok et al. (2021)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sfiligoi et al. (2020)</a></cite>; thus, we consider two cloud network configurations with different performance.
We summarize detailed network performance parameters in <a href="#S4.T7" title="In 4.8 Device-Server Collaborative Inference ‣ 4 Evaluation and Takeaways ‣ How Fast Can I Run My VLA? Demystifying VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS7.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS7.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS7.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_ulem_uline ltx_font_italic">Takeaway 9: Server-side inference, even with only consumer GPUs, significantly outperforms on-device inference in most scenarios, except under extremely poor network conditions.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS7.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS7.p3.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in <a href="#S4.F8" title="In 4.8 Device-Server Collaborative Inference ‣ 4 Evaluation and Takeaways ‣ How Fast Can I Run My VLA? Demystifying VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>, even when using a consumer GPU (RTX 4090) connected via WiFi, server-side inference achieves lower end-to-end latency than on-device inference on Jetson Thor.
With a more powerful B100 GPU, inference remains faster than on-device execution even when deployed on an edge server with only cellular (5G) connectivity or in a cloud instance with fast network.
On-device inference becomes preferable only when network conditions are extremely constrained, such as (i) slow cellular connections (4G or below), or (ii) cloud deployments where the datacenter is distant from the robot.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS8" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.8 </span>Device-Server Collaborative Inference</h3>

<div id="S4.SS8.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS8.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Some robots already have an on-board GPU — so a natural idea is to split the VLA workload between server and device to (1) reduce server workloads and to (2) improve performance over device-only deployments.
Since the action expert model is usually several times smaller than the VLM backbone <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Black et al. (2024)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shukor et al. (2025)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wen et al. (2025a)</a></cite>, a natural idea is to run VLM inference (including the vision encoder) on server (B100) and run action expert inference on device (Jetson Thor).
In comparison to either device-only or server-only solutions, here, device-server collaboration involves an extra communication step, where the KV cache of the VLM has to be downloaded to the device GPU before action prediction begins.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS8.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS8.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS8.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_ulem_uline ltx_font_italic">Takeaway 10. Device–server collaboration is often slower than device-only inference and always slower than server-side inference, making this solution generally unattractive in practice.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS8.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS8.p3.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in <a href="#S4.F9" title="In 4.8 Device-Server Collaborative Inference ‣ 4 Evaluation and Takeaways ‣ How Fast Can I Run My VLA? Demystifying VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>, collaborative inference is always slower compared to server-only inference — which is not surprising as now the action expert runs on a less powerful device.
What we found interesting is that it is even slower than on-device inference in most cases, except with a fast wired network (Ethernet 10G) — this is because of the KV cache download process from the server to the device, which can be very slow without a fast network (12.4, 43.7, and 257.7 ms for Ethernet 10G, WiFI 7, and 5G networks, respectively).
However, we argue that such scenarios are rare in practice: robots equipped with on-device GPUs are typically mobile platforms that relies on wireless connectivity, in which case using the on-device GPU alone (rather than device-server collaboration) is the more performant choice.</p>
</div>

<section id="S4.SS9" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.9 </span>Asynchronous Inference</h3>

<div id="S4.SS9.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS9.p1.1" class="ltx_p">With asynchronous inference, the model predicts actions based on stale observations rather than the latest state, allowing model inference and robot action execution to be partially overlapped.
While this form of asynchrony does not increase the maximum inference throughput for on-device inference without network latency, it can benefit server-side inference by allowing network transmission and GPU computation to proceed concurrently.
Thus, the asynchronous inference throughput is bounded by the minimum of GPU inference throughput and network transmission throughput.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS9.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS9.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS9.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_ulem_uline ltx_font_italic">Takeaway 11: Asynchrony between robot execution and inference can significantly improve system throughput for server-side inference, especially under slow wireless network connections.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS9.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS9.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#S4.T8" title="In 4.9 Asynchronous Inference ‣ 4 Evaluation and Takeaways ‣ How Fast Can I Run My VLA? Demystifying VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> reports the server-side inference throughput under different network configurations.
With fast wired networks (e.g., 1 GbE and 10 GbE Ethernet), synchronous and asynchronous inference achieve similar throughput.
In contrast, under slower wireless networks (WiFi 7, 5G, and 4G), asynchronous inference improves throughput by 2.63<math id="S4.SS9.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>5.99<math id="S4.SS9.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math>.
With WiFi 7, inference remains GPU-bound, and thus achieves the same throughput to wired networks (314.4Hz).
For 5G and 4G, the bottleneck shifts to network transmission, resulting in lower asynchronous throughput.
Note that while asynchronous inference improves throughput, it does not reduce end-to-end latency; increased staleness may degrade action quality, which warrants further investigation from the perspective of control stability and task success rate.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T8" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S4.T8.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 8</span>: </span><span id="S4.T8.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Inference frequency of synchronous and asynchronous systems.</span></figcaption>
<div id="S4.T8.5" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_transformed_outer" style="width:342.3pt;height:99.8pt;vertical-align:-47.8pt;"><span class="ltx_transformed_inner" style="transform:translate(-30.2pt,8.8pt) scale(0.8,0.8) ;">
<table id="S4.T8.5.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_middle">
<tr id="S4.T8.5.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S4.T8.5.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_middle ltx_border_tt">
<span id="S4.T8.5.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_middle" style="width:50.0pt;">
<span id="S4.T8.5.1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_left"><span id="S4.T8.5.1.1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Hardware</span></span>
</span></td>

<section id="S4.SS10" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.10 </span>Dual-system VLA Pipelines</h3>

<div id="S4.SS10.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS10.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Recent work proposes a <span id="S4.SS10.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">System 1 + System 2</span> paradigm for action generation, where a slower System 2 (the VLM) responsible for high-level reasoning operates at a lower frequency (e.g., 5–10 Hz), while a faster System 1 (the action model) reacts to the environment at a higher frequency using the most recent visual inputs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Figure AI (2025)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al. (2024)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Song et al. (2025)</a></cite>.
The two systems run asynchronously: the action expert conditions its predictions on the VLM’s KV cache, which is updated at a lower frequency by System 2.
While this design is conceptually appealing, we are not aware of a widely adopted, open-source diffusion-style implementation of a dual-system VLA.
Therefore, we make the following approximations in our evaluation:
(1) System 1 latency consists of image upload, vision encoding, diffusion-based action prediction, and action download, where the cost of integrating vision features into the action expert is assumed to be negligible; and
(2) System 2 latency equals VLM inference, which incorporates the visual encoding of the most recently uploaded image.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS10.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS10.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS10.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_ulem_uline ltx_font_italic">Takeaway 12: Asynchronous inference between System 1 and System 2 can improve action prediction performance, with performance gains strongly dependent on hardware capability and network latency.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS10.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS10.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#S4.T9" title="In 4.10 Dual-system VLA Pipelines ‣ 4 Evaluation and Takeaways ‣ How Fast Can I Run My VLA? Demystifying VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> reports performance across different system configurations and System 2 frequency caps (5 Hz and 10 Hz).
On Jetson Thor, the improvement is moderate (1.46<math id="S4.SS10.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> at a 5 Hz cap and 1.30<math id="S4.SS10.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> at a 10 Hz cap), since the asynchronous frequency cap is comparable to the synchronous VLM frequency of 19 Hz.
In contrast, on B100 with a fast 10G Ethernet connection, the speedup is substantial (2.24<math id="S4.SS10.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> at a 10 Hz cap).
In this case, asynchronous execution significantly reduces the effective VLM invocation rate from 301.4 Hz to 10 Hz, freeing compute resources that can be reallocated to action prediction.
However, under slower network conditions (e.g., 5G), the benefit diminishes, yielding only a 1.05<math id="S4.SS10.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> speedup at a 10 Hz cap.
This is because network latency substantially increases System 1 latency — from 1.5 ms with Ethernet to 26.0 ms with 5G — thereby limiting the achievable performance regardless of the inference hardware capability.</p>
</div>

</section>
<section id="S4.SS11" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.11 </span>Supporting High-Performance VLA Inference up to 100 Hz</h3>

<div id="S4.SS11.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS11.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we analyze how 10 Hz and 100 Hz performance targets (§<a href="#S2" title="2 Background and Motivation ‣ How Fast Can I Run My VLA? Demystifying VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>) can be achieved with the <math id="S4.SS11.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> model across on-device, edge-server, and cloud-server inference systems.
We also discuss what algorithm-level adjustments may be required when the target performance cannot be met by those systems.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS11.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS11.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS11.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_ulem_uline ltx_font_italic">Takeaway 13: For on-device inference, the most advanced edge GPUs (Jetson Thor) can already achieve 10 Hz inference for <math id="S4.SS11.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>, but reaching 100 Hz requires model-level adjustments.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS11.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS11.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#S4.T3" title="In 4.2 Baseline 𝜋_0 Inference Latency Across Hardware Backends ‣ 4 Evaluation and Takeaways ‣ How Fast Can I Run My VLA? Demystifying VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> shows that Jetson Thor already achieves 19 Hz inference throughput for <math id="S4.SS11.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>, exceeding the 10 Hz target.
However, achieving 100 Hz would require roughly a <math id="S4.SS11.p3.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="5\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5\times</annotation></semantics></math> improvement.
This gap have to be closed through model-level optimizations, such as reducing model size (§<a href="#S4.SS3" title="4.3 Scaling Model Sizes Under Real-Time Constraints ‣ 4 Evaluation and Takeaways ‣ How Fast Can I Run My VLA? Demystifying VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3</span></a>), decreasing the number of diffusion steps (§<a href="#S4.SS5" title="4.5 Impact of Denoising Steps and Action Chunk Size ‣ 4 Evaluation and Takeaways ‣ How Fast Can I Run My VLA? Demystifying VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.5</span></a>), or using lower-precision quantization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al. (2024)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al. (2025a)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS11.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS11.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS11.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_ulem_uline ltx_font_italic">Takeaway 14: For edge-server inference, 10 Hz is achievable with consumer GPUs and wireless networks, while 100 Hz requires datacenter GPUs and faster networks.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS11.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS11.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#S4.F8" title="In 4.8 Device-Server Collaborative Inference ‣ 4 Evaluation and Takeaways ‣ How Fast Can I Run My VLA? Demystifying VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> shows that an RTX 4090 can achieve 10 Hz inference even with a slow 4G network.
However, achieving sub-10 ms latency (100 Hz) requires either a more powerful accelerator such as B100 or the aforementioned model-level optimizations.
For B100, reaching 100 Hz further depends on network performance, requiring either wired Ethernet or high-quality wireless connectivity (e.g., WiFi 7).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS11.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS11.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS11.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_ulem_uline ltx_font_italic">Takeaway 15: For cloud-server inference, 10 Hz is feasible with good networking, while achieving 100 Hz generally requires asynchronous inference.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS11.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS11.p7.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in <a href="#S4.T8" title="In 4.9 Asynchronous Inference ‣ 4 Evaluation and Takeaways ‣ How Fast Can I Run My VLA? Demystifying VLA Inference Performance with VLA-Perf" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>, B100 achieves only 42.8 Hz under synchronous cloud inference even with a fast network.
In this regime, network latency alone (exceeding 10 ms per upload or download) prevents achieving 100 Hz, making computation reduction insufficient and rendering asynchronous inference necessary for high-frequency operation.
With a fast network (WiFi 7 or better), asynchronous execution cab achieve a throughput of 314.4 Hz.
Even under poor network conditions where synchronous inference becomes unacceptable (3.7 Hz), asynchronous inference can still restore acceptable performance (50.5 Hz).</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Conclusion and Future Work</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We present the first comprehensive study of VLA inference performance.
Using <span id="S5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">VLA-Perf</span>, an analytical performance modeling tool that we develop, we systematically explore a wide range of (1) model configurations, including model size, context length, architectural choices, and synchronous versus asynchronous execution, and (2) system configurations spanning different hardware platforms, inference placements, and network conditions.
From the performance study, we distill 15 key takeaways that provide practical guidance for the design of future VLA models and inference systems.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">While this work represents an important step toward understanding and building next-generation VLA systems, we view it as only a starting point.
First, our study focuses primarily on VLA models for manipulation tasks and does not consider other embodied AI domains such as autonomous driving, quadrupeds, or drones.
These settings often involve different system constraints (e.g., stronger emphasis on on-device execution) and additional model components (e.g., SLAM and specialized control modules), which are beyond the scope of this work.
Second, robotic systems are complex end-to-end pipelines that go beyond model inference alone.
In this work, we do not account for robot execution latency or sensor latency (e.g., cameras), as these factors vary widely across platforms.
A more comprehensive performance analysis that integrates inference, sensing, and actuation would provide deeper insights into end-to-end robotic system behavior.
We leave these directions to future work.</p>
</div>
</section>

    <p>Our team has already identified <a class="ltx_ref" href="https://github.com/arXiv/html_feedback/issues"
        target="_blank">the following issues</a>. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we
      may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability
      should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for
      all.</p>
